Conveniently located at 10213 Kingston Pike in Knoxville, our AAHA-accredited emergency and specialty veterinary hospital provides compassionate, state-of-the-art emergency care, critical care, internal medicine, surgery, oncology, anesthesia, diagnostic imaging, and advanced specialty care.

Emergency services are available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, including walk-ins, urgent cases, and immediate veterinary referrals. Specialty referral services are available Monday through Friday during regular business hours.

Trusted by pet owners and referring veterinarians and throughout Tennessee, our hospital is staffed by experienced emergency clinicians and board-certified specialists who work together to provide exceptional patient care. On-site veterinarians are available around the clock, supported by a highly trained nursing and support team, ensuring pets receive timely, expert care at every hour of the day.

Knoxville families and referring veterinarians throughout East Tennessee praise our hospital for compassionate, expert, and around-the-clock emergency and specialty veterinary care.

## Veterinarians, you can trust our work.

When you refer a patient to us, we recognize that you’re placing confidence in your reputation and our ability to treat your patient successfully. We do everything we can to ensure a positive experience for your client from beginning to end.

We have the expertise to provide support for your patients in the following areas:

  * Emergency
  * Critical care
  * Internal medicine
  * Surgery
  * Oncology
  * Diagnostic imaging
  * Radiation treatment

If you have a particular case you need help with, we encourage you to contact us right away.

Refer a patient

### Emergency

24/7 emergency veterinary care for dogs, cats, and exotic pets across Knoxville and East Tennessee. Our on-site emergency team is ready around the clock for walk-ins, life-threatening illness, trauma, toxin exposure, and other urgent situations. No appointment needed.

### Critical Care

Advanced critical care for the most fragile patients, including 24-hour intensive monitoring, oxygen therapy, IV fluid and medication management, and continuous support for pets recovering from surgery, trauma, or severe illness.

### Internal Medicine

Board-certified internal medicine for the diagnosis and management of complex conditions affecting the gastrointestinal, endocrine, respiratory, urinary, and immune systems; partnering closely with your primary care veterinarian for seamless treatment plans.

### Surgery

Soft-tissue, orthopedic, and emergency surgical procedures performed by experienced veterinary surgeons in our modern, AAHA-accredited surgical suite, with careful pre-op planning, advanced anesthesia monitoring, and attentive post-op recovery.

### Oncology

Compassionate cancer care for dogs and cats, including diagnostics, staging, chemotherapy, and quality-of-life-focused treatment planning, helping East Tennessee families navigate a difficult diagnosis with expertise and empathy.

UTCVM VETERINARY MEDICAL CENTER — SMALL ANIMAL HOSPITAL

UTCVM ONCOLOGY SERVICE

# Chemotherapy for dogs & cats

## What is chemotherapy?
Chemotherapy drugs are medications that kill cancer cells. These drugs are usually given intravenously (into the vein) on an outpatient basis, but some are available as a daily pill that can be given at home. The goal of chemotherapy is to control your pet’s cancer and to prolong survival while maintaining a good quality of life at home.

## When is chemotherapy used?
Chemotherapy is typically used in the following circumstances in cats and dogs:
- For pets with cancers in which chemotherapy is the treatment of choice (i.e. lymphoma)
- After surgical removal of a primary tumor which has a high likelihood of spreading to other areas of the body (i.e. bone cancer)
- For pets with large tumors that cannot be surgically removed in which the goal is to delay growth and control clinical signs (i.e. large and/or metastatic mast cell tumors)
- To enhance the effects of radiation therapy on tumor tissues (i.e. several types of sarcoma)

## What side effects can chemotherapy cause in dogs and cats?
Because our priority is to maintain good quality of life, we use doses and schedules of chemotherapy with the goal of avoiding side effects. Most chemotherapy agents work by affecting rapidly dividing cells, so the cells of the GI tract and the bone marrow can be affected. 80-85% of our patients have minimal to no side effects from chemotherapy, while about 15-20% of patients may have side effects that require treatment. However the incidence of requiring hospitalization from side effects is less than 5%. We typically send home medications to treat nausea and diarrhea for use as needed. We also monitor our patient’s blood cell counts on a routine basis; if the white blood cell count drops too low, we prescribe antibiotics to help protect against potential infection.

While most dogs and cats do not have any hair loss secondary to chemotherapy, clipped fur may regrow slowly. Some breeds that require grooming, such as poodles, schnauzers, and Bichon frise, can develop hair loss or skin pigment change to varying degrees. Additionally, cats may lose their whiskers. Lost hair will usually regrow after discontinuation of chemotherapy, although it may differ in color and texture.

Overall, most veterinary patients tolerate chemotherapy very well. Today your doctor may discuss potential chemotherapy options for your pet, and we will answer any questions you have regarding chemotherapy use in your pet.

# Allison Mallard

Diplomate American College of Veterinary Internal Medicine (Oncology)

Dr. Allison Mallard is a native of Nashville and received her Bachelor of Science in animal medicine from Middle Tennessee State University. She went on to earn her DVM from the University of Tennessee, Knoxville. After graduation, she completed an internship with Kansas State University, for small animal medicine and surgery.

Returning to Knoxville, Dr. Mallard completed a 3-year residency for veterinary oncology. Her residency involved the treatment of canine visceral hemangiosarcoma with modified metronomic chemotherapy. Dr. Mallard's special interests include lymphoma, hemangiosarcoma, and urothelial carcinoma.

Outside of work, she enjoys spending time with her husband, antiquing, watching home remodel shows, and traveling. She and her husband have two scruffy dogs, Gidget and Prim, and a calico cat, Tippie.

# Chemotherapy

Chemotherapy, also known as chemo, is the treatment of cancer with one or more drugs. Chemotherapy may be used to try to cure a pet of cancer, prolong his or her life, or simply make his or her symptoms less severe. Chemotherapy may be used in conjunction with other treatment modes, such as surgery and/or radiation therapy.
Chemotherapy drugs work by killing cancer cells (cells that divide rapidly), and as such may also harm cells that are supposed to divide rapidly -- cells of bone marrow, the digestive tract, and hair follicles.

### Partnering with Your Client

As your hamster veterinarian in Nashville, we are fostering open communication and realistic expectations is crucial:

  * Educate owners: Clearly explain the different types of lymphoma, diagnostic procedures, and available treatment options.
  * Manage expectations: Emphasize the limitations of HaPV treatment and the potential for recurrence in other forms.
  * Provide supportive guidance: Offer practical advice on medication administration, monitoring for side effects, and establishing quality-of-life parameters.
 

### Vigilance is Key

Early detection is paramount. Encourage owners to be vigilant for any changes in their hamster's behavior, including:

  * Decreased appetite
  * Vomiting or diarrhea
  * Excessive thirst or urination
  * Unexplained weight loss
  * Lethargy or weakness
  * Palpable masses

### A Collaborative Approach

By acknowledging the complexities of lymphoma in hamsters and fostering a collaborative approach, we can empower owners to navigate this challenging disease with knowledge, compassion, and hope. The oncology program prides itself on having a high level of expertise through its faculty and staff, consisting of Dr. Kenita Rogers, Dr. Claudia Barton, Dr. Zachary Wright and Krystal Schneider.

The CVM recently welcomed Dr. Heather Wilson to the faculty, as the latest oncologist added to the team fighting cancer. She received her DVM from the University of Tennessee in 2003 then completed a small animal rotating internship at the University of Minnesota Veterinary Medical Center and a residency in Medical Oncology at the University of Wisconsin-Madison, Veterinary Teaching Hospital. She is a Diplomate of the American College of Veterinary Internal Medicine in the specialty of Oncology and recipient of the E. Gregory MacEwen award for Outstanding Basic Science Research in the field of Oncology from the Veterinary Cancer Society in 2006. Her research and clinical interests include cancer stem cells, osteosarcoma, and transitional cell carcinoma.

Dr. Wilson is looking forward to conducting clinical trials and is hoping to bring A&M to the forefront of the fight against cancer. Dr. Wilson explained that Texas A&M University has completed the application process to join the Comparative Oncology Clinical Trial Consortium, which is a division of the National Cancer Institute, and is awaiting approval.
